ov_en: "Remember Me" persistent login vulnerabilities involve reversible token generation, predictable keys, and deserialization risks. Attackers who analyze or forge these tokens achieve persistent identity impersonation. Apache Shiro RememberMe deserialization (CVE-2016-4437) is a classic example.
vu_en: Common flaws: reversible encoding (Base64) instead of encrypted signatures; default or hardcoded encryption key; Java/PHP serialized objects in Cookie leading to RCE on deserialization; Cookie not bound to client fingerprint and replayable cross-device; excessively long lifetime with no forced revocation.
ex_en: Obtain and analyze Remember-Me Cookie (Base64 decode, hex inspect). Check for known framework format and test default key. Analyze whether Cookie contains a modifiable user identifier. Test Java deserialization (replace Cookie with ysoserial payload). Test cross-IP/device Cookie replay.
mi_en: Use cryptographically secure random token as identifier; never store user info in Cookie; change framework default encryption keys; prohibit serialized objects in Cookies; bind token to client fingerprint; set reasonable lifetime (max 30 days); provide logout-all-devices for token revocation.

ov_en: JWT None Algorithm Attack (CVE-2015-2951) is the most classic JWT security vulnerability. The JWT spec defines "none" to indicate no signature is needed. Many JWT libraries accept the client-specified algorithm; when an attacker changes alg to none and removes the signature, the server skips verification and trusts the payload directly.
vu_en: Root cause: (1) JWT library supports none algorithm with no application-level explicit disabling; (2) Verification logic uses the client-supplied alg from the Header rather than server-configured algorithm; (3) Some libraries do case-sensitive matching on none but are bypassed by None/NONE variants; (4) Signature verification returns true when signature is empty.
ex_en: 1. Obtain a valid JWT (e.g., register a normal account) 2. Base64-decode Header and Payload 3. Change alg field to none 4. Modify Payload (e.g., role to admin) 5. Re-encode as header.payload. (empty signature) 6. Use forged JWT to access privileged endpoints. Use jwt_tool -X a to automatically test all none variants.
mi_en: 1. Hardcode allowed signing algorithm allowlist server-side, explicitly disable none 2. Use server-configured algorithm for verification, not Header alg 3. Upgrade JWT library (modern libraries reject none by default) 4. Implement JWT signing key rotation 5. Add JWT token blacklist to support logout/revocation.

ov_en: JWT Key Confusion (Algorithm Confusion) attack exploits JWT libraries that trust the alg field in the Header during signature verification. When the server is configured for RS256 (asymmetric), an attacker changes alg to HS256 (symmetric); the server then attempts to verify the HMAC signature using the RSA public key. Since the RSA public key is public, the attacker can compute a valid HMAC signature.
vu_en: Vulnerability chain: (1) Server uses RS256; (2) RSA public key is typically obtainable from /.well-known/jwks.json or certificate; (3) Attacker changes alg to HS256 in JWT Header; (4) Server verification logic uses Header alg to decide method; (5) HS256 uses the "key" as HMAC—that "key" is the RSA public key. Root cause: algorithm selection is client-side, not server-side.
ex_en: 1. Confirm target JWT uses RS256/RS384/RS512 2. Obtain RSA public key from JWKS endpoint, OAuth discovery, or SSL certificate 3. Change JWT Header alg to HS256 4. Sign the modified JWT using the obtained RSA public key as HMAC secret 5. Note public key format—may need PEM, DER, or stripped newlines. jwt_tool -X k automates the process.
mi_en: 1. Hardcode allowed algorithm list server-side; never use Header alg for verification 2. Use type-safe verification functions specifying algorithms=["RS256"] 3. Upgrade JWT library to latest version 4. If using JWKS, restrict key retrieval to trusted URLs, disable jku/x5u redirects 5. Rotate signing keys regularly.

ov_en: JWT HMAC secret brute-force attacks target JWT systems using symmetric signing algorithms (HS256/HS384/HS512). Since HMAC uses a shared secret for both signing and verification, weak secrets (short passwords, common words, default values) can be recovered via dictionary or brute-force attack—then used to forge arbitrary JWTs.
vu_en: Vulnerability conditions: (1) JWT uses HMAC algorithm; (2) Signing secret is a weak password (e.g., secret, 123456); (3) Key not rotated; (4) Using default example keys from jwt.io in production. JWT spec recommends HS256 keys of at least 256 bits (32 bytes) random data, but many systems use short human-readable passwords. A consumer GPU can test billions of HS256 keys per second.
ex_en: 1. Obtain a valid JWT sample from login response or Cookie 2. Decode and confirm HS256/384/512 algorithm 3. Use hashcat -m 16500 with a large wordlist (rockyou.txt) for GPU-accelerated cracking 4. Or use jwt_tool -C -d to quickly test common weak secrets 5. After cracking, sign arbitrary payload JWTs with the recovered secret 6. An RTX 4090 can exhaust the rockyou list (14M entries) within minutes.
mi_en: 1. Use at least 256-bit cryptographically secure random secret (openssl rand -hex 32) 2. Prefer asymmetric algorithms (RS256/ES256) to avoid shared secret issues 3. Rotate JWT signing secrets regularly 4. Never deploy with default/example keys 5. Implement JWT expiry (exp) and blacklist to limit leaked token impact.

ov_en: JKU (JWK Set URL) and X5U (X.509 URL) are optional JWT Header parameters specifying the URL of the verification key. If the server fetches the public key from jku/x5u in the Header without URL restriction, attackers can point it to their own server—making the server use the attacker's public key to verify an attacker-signed JWT.
vu_en: Root cause: (1) Server trusts the URL in the jku/x5u Header parameter; (2) No URL allowlist or domain restriction; (3) Domain validation can be bypassed via open redirects or subdomain takeover; (4) Some implementations even allow HTTP (non-HTTPS) jku URLs. Attacker generates their own RSA key pair, signs JWT with private key, and hosts the corresponding JWKS public key file publicly.
ex_en: Complete attack chain: (1) Decode target JWT, confirm RS256 and jku field in Header; (2) Generate attacker RSA key pair; (3) Convert public key to JWKS format and host on attacker server; (4) Modify JWT Header jku to point to attacker server; (5) Sign tampered Payload with attacker private key; (6) Send forged JWT—server fetches key from attacker URL and verifies successfully. If domain allowlist exists, bypass via open redirect or subdomain takeover.
mi_en: 1. Disable jku/x5u Header parameters; hardcode key source in server config 2. If jku is required, enforce strict URL allowlist with no redirect following 3. Pin JWKS public keys in server config rather than dynamic fetching 4. Map kid to known keys; reject unknown kid values 5. Regularly audit JWT library config to ensure client-supplied key sources are not trusted.

ov_en: Package name typosquatting is one of the most common supply chain attack techniques. Attackers register malicious packages on NPM/PyPI with names highly similar to popular packages, exploiting developer typos during installation. The ua-parser-js and colors/faker poisoning incidents in 2022 demonstrated the severe impact of this attack surface.
vu_en: Root causes: (1) NPM registry does not restrict registration of names similar to existing packages; (2) Developers frequently make typos when manually typing package names; (3) postinstall and other lifecycle hooks execute automatically during installation with no sandbox isolation; (4) Most developers do not audit node_modules code; (5) CI/CD pipelines typically run npm install with elevated privileges.
ex_en: Attack chain: (1) Select high-download-count target packages and generate typosquatting variants; (2) Create malicious package copying the original's functionality to avoid detection; (3) Inject malicious code in preinstall/postinstall hooks (steal env variables/SSH keys/install backdoors); (4) Publish to NPM and wait for victims to install; (5) Collect stolen credentials via C2 server; (6) Use obtained CI/CD credentials to further compromise the supply chain.
mi_en: 1. Use --ignore-scripts to disable install hooks: npm install --ignore-scripts 2. Enable npm audit and third-party scanners (Snyk/Socket.dev) 3. Use package-lock.json to pin versions and npm ci in CI 4. Configure .npmrc scope restrictions and private registry 5. Principle of least privilege: CI/CD environments do not expose unnecessary secrets.

ov_en: CI/CD pipeline poisoning is the highest-impact supply chain attack technique. GitHub Actions, Jenkins, and GitLab CI typically hold deployment keys and cloud credentials. In the 2021 Codecov breach, attackers stole environment variables from thousands of companies by tampering with CI scripts. pull_request_target and expression injection are the most common GitHub Actions attack surfaces.
vu_en: Root causes: (1) pull_request_target event executes forked code in the main repository context with access to Secrets; (2) GitHub Actions ${{}} expressions unsafely interpolate user input (PR title/issue comments) into shell commands; (3) Developers lack auditing of third-party Actions—malicious Actions can steal all Secrets; (4) Build logs may leak keys even if masked (bypassable via encoding); (5) CI environment often has unrestricted network access.
ex_en: Attack chain: (1) Search target repository's .github/workflows directory for workflow configs; (2) Identify workflows using pull_request_target—these are triggered by PRs and have Secrets access; (3) Craft malicious PR to access main repo Secrets via the checkout step; (4) If no pull_request_target, attempt expression injection via PR title/body; (5) Use obtained Secrets to further attack deployment targets.
mi_en: 1. Avoid pull_request_target; if required, do not checkout PR code 2. Pass all user input via environment variables rather than direct ${{}} interpolation 3. Pin third-party Actions to specific SHA not tags (actions/checkout@a1b2c3d) 4. Enable GitHub Required Reviewers to block unreviewed workflow modifications 5. Use OpenSSF Scorecard to assess supply chain security posture.

ov_en: Dependency Confusion was discovered and disclosed by researcher Alex Birsan in 2021, affecting tech giants including Apple, Microsoft, and PayPal. It exploits package managers (NPM/PyPI/RubyGems) preferring higher-versioned packages from public registries over private ones for the same package name. Attackers only need to know an internal package name to publish a same-named higher-versioned malicious package publicly.
vu_en: Root causes: (1) NPM and similar package managers query both public and private registries and prefer the higher version; (2) Many enterprises have misconfigured .npmrc registry scope mappings; (3) Internal package names can be discovered via leaked lock files, JS source code, GitHub searches, or error messages; (4) CI/CD pipelines automatically run npm install with network access; (5) Loose version ranges in package.json (e.g., ^1.0.0) more easily match higher versions.
ex_en: Attack flow: (1) Discover internal package names via JS source, lock file leaks, or GitHub searches; (2) Confirm the name is not registered on NPM public registry; (3) Create same-named public package with version 99.x.x; (4) Embed DNS/HTTP callback code to confirm installation (no destructive action); (5) Wait for target CI/CD or developer's npm install to trigger; (6) Confirm via DNS/HTTP callback and collect target environment information.
mi_en: 1. Configure .npmrc scope pointing to private registry: @company:registry=https://private.registry.com 2. Register all internal package names in the private registry even if only used internally 3. Use --prefer-offline and package-lock.json to pin versions 4. Enable npm audit and Dependabot for anomalous dependency detection 5. Enforce strict version pinning in CI/CD.

ov_en: Prototype Pollution is a JavaScript-specific vulnerability exploiting JS prototype inheritance. When an application uses unsafe deep merge (lodash.merge/deepmerge, etc.) to merge user input into an object, attackers can pollute Object.prototype via the __proto__ property, affecting all subsequently created objects. Combined with specific template engine gadget chains (EJS/Pug), this achieves RCE.
vu_en: Root cause: (1) Almost all JS objects inherit from Object.prototype; (2) Recursive merge functions do not filter __proto__/constructor/prototype keys; (3) Popular libraries like lodash (<4.17.12), jQuery, and merge-deep are vulnerable; (4) Server-side Node.js with EJS/Pug template engines has known RCE gadget chains; (5) JSON.parse does not filter __proto__ keys.
ex_en: 1. Identify API endpoints that accept JSON input and perform object merging (PUT /settings, PATCH /profile) 2. Send __proto__ pollution test payload to confirm vulnerability 3. Select gadget chain for the target stack—EJS uses outputFunctionName/escapeFunction, Pug uses block property 4. Craft RCE payload injected into __proto__ 5. Trigger the gadget chain to execute commands.
mi_en: 1. Use Object.create(null) to create prototype-less safe objects 2. Filter __proto__, constructor, prototype keys in merge functions 3. Upgrade lodash to 4.17.21+ 4. Use Map instead of plain objects for user input storage 5. Enforce JSON Schema validation on JSON input, reject requests containing __proto__ 6. Enable --disable-proto=throw in Node.js.

ov_en: Client-side prototype pollution is triggered in the browser via URL parameters, postMessage, and similar vectors. Unlike server-side pollution, client-side pollution typically requires a "gadget"—code that reads the polluted property—to cause real harm (e.g., XSS). Popular frontend libraries like jQuery, Lodash, and DOMPurify have known gadget chains.
vu_en: Root causes: (1) Custom URL parameter parsers converting ?a[b]=c to nested objects without filtering __proto__; (2) Old versions of qs and query-string libraries have prototype pollution vulnerabilities; (3) jQuery $.extend(true,...), lodash.merge, and other deep copy functions propagate pollution; (4) DOMPurify configuration can be overridden by prototype pollution; (5) Frontend frameworks may read polluted properties.
ex_en: 1. Check if target page uses custom query parser or known vulnerable library 2. Send __proto__[test]=1 via URL param and verify ({}).test===1 in console 3. If pollution succeeds, search page code for gadgets—code that reads specific property names 4. Common gadgets: jQuery html() reads innerHTML, DOMPurify reads ALLOWED_ATTR 5. Chain pollution with gadget to trigger XSS.
mi_en: 1. Use patched URL param parsing library (qs@6.10.0+) 2. Object.freeze(Object.prototype) to prevent pollution (check compatibility) 3. Upgrade jQuery, Lodash, etc. to latest versions 4. Use Object.create(null) when creating objects 5. Whitelist URL parameter names; reject params containing __proto__/constructor 6. Use strict CSP to limit inline script execution.

ov_en: Combining prototype pollution with NoSQL injection is an advanced exploit technique. Standalone prototype pollution may require a template engine gadget for RCE; standalone NoSQL injection may be blocked by operator filtering. Combined, prototype pollution can bypass query validation logic, injecting malicious MongoDB operators into otherwise safe queries.
vu_en: Root causes: (1) Node.js backend uses lodash.merge for config/settings update requests, introducing prototype pollution; (2) MongoDB query construction has no strict type checking on input values (allowing objects as query values); (3) Backend operator filtering only checks direct properties, not prototype chain inherited properties; (4) Express.js automatically converts URL query params like password[$ne]= to nested objects {password:{$ne:""}}; (5) Mongo operator checks do not account for prototype chain.
ex_en: 1. Test pure NoSQL injection first—send $ne/$gt operators and observe response differences 2. If blocked by WAF or validation, find prototype pollution entry points (PUT /settings, PATCH /config) 3. Inject $where or override query validation properties via prototype pollution 4. Resend login request using polluted prototype chain to bypass operator checks 5. Use obtained admin token to further enumerate user data 6. Use $regex blind injection to extract password hashes.
mi_en: 1. Strict type validation on all JSON input (Joi/Zod schema validation) 2. Use mongo-sanitize or similar to filter $ operators from queries 3. Disable MongoDB $where operator (--setParameter disableJavaScript=true) 4. Fix prototype pollution: upgrade lodash/use Object.create(null)/filter __proto__ 5. Use parameterized queries where possible.

ov_en: Cloud SSRF for metadata credential theft is one of the most impactful attack surfaces in recent years. The 2019 Capital One breach (100M+ users affected) was achieved via SSRF to AWS IMDS to obtain IAM credentials. Cloud instance metadata services (169.254.169.254) provide temporary credentials, user-data, and network configuration. A web application SSRF allows attackers to pivot from the web tier directly to cloud infrastructure.
vu_en: Root causes: (1) AWS IMDSv1 requires no authentication (internal network only); (2) Web application SSRF allows requests to internal network addresses; (3) EC2 instance bound to an overly permissive IAM role (violates least privilege); (4) Secrets/passwords hardcoded in user-data; (5) Even with IMDSv2 (requires PUT for token), some SSRF scenarios (e.g., header injection) can still bypass it; (6) GCP/Azure header protections are bypassable in some configurations.
ex_en: 1. Discover SSRF (URL param, webhook, file import entry points) 2. Request http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ to confirm cloud environment 3. Get IAM role name: /iam/security-credentials/ 4. Obtain temporary credentials (AccessKeyId+SecretAccessKey+Token) 5. Configure AWS CLI with credentials and enumerate permissions 6. Enumerate accessible S3 buckets, RDS, Lambda, and other resources.
mi_en: 1. Enforce IMDSv2 (aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --http-tokens required) 2. Fix SSRF: URL allowlist/block internal addresses 3. IAM role least privilege 4. Use VPC endpoints to restrict IMDS access 5. Enable GuardDuty to detect anomalous API calls 6. Never store sensitive info in user-data 7. Use IMDSv2 token-required mode for all instances.
